utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can everyone hear me? Are there no problems? Any problems regarding the hearing. General Blaskic, can you hear me too?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Very well, in that case we can continue with the hearing of the witness, which started yesterday, and who is planned for three hours, maybe less if we focus on the questions affecting the crux of the matter as Mr. Cayley has been doing. So can we have Captain Tudor Ellis brought in, please, Mr. Registrar. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Can you hear me, Captain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest, are you feeling fit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we can begin then. CAPTAIN TUDOR ELLIS (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, your Honours, learned counsel. Good morning, Captain Ellis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would just like to very briefly recap where we left off yesterday, go back over what we were speaking about yesterday. I think you had stated at the end of yesterday's hearing that you had come to a checkpoint in the northern area of the town. I wondered if you could stand and pick up the pointer and just indicate to the court the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The checkpoint was in the area of the junction here, just about there. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the British battalion was actually used to passing another checkpoint in the northern area of town, this checkpoint was not the usual checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would be correct in saying that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that checkpoint located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That checkpoint was located on the Zenica mountain road, and if you actually follow this road up here, the junction -- there was a checkpoint there manning the junction to the Zenica mountain road there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you take a pen and actually mark the location of the checkpoint on this particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could mark that "HVO 2". If you could take a seat now, please. From the location of this checkpoint I think you will recall that you said that you saw two squads, two organised military formations of men walking into the centre of town, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were the numbers of these two squads of men approximately as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two squads of men, one on either side of the road, the first one was approximately about 10 people and then the second one was approximately 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you also stated that there was a number of troops behind the checkpoint that were, as it were, marshalling or organising themselves to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, all this has already been stated by the witness, I think, at the end of the afternoon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I was just, for the benefit of the court, recalling the testimony of yesterday. We can move straight ahead if you wish, Mr. President. I do not wish to waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thank you for the benefit of the judges, but the Tribunal has been informed by the witness, so perhaps we can go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Approximately what time was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would have been at approximately 7.15 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that these troops would not actually allow you to pass the checkpoint, so what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I decided to turn around, move back down the bypass road and then come into the town of Vitez from the southern end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just indicate on the map the road in which you went into the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved back down this road here. It is not actually shown on this photograph. There is a junction about here, I moved up and then proceeded into the town from the southern end, along the main Vitez road there. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could remain standing, because this part of your testimony is quite complex. A number of different incidents happened and I will try to make this as clear as possible. What was the first point where you came to a halt in the town, where you actually stopped and looked around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drove into the town, I moved past the garage, which is located here (indicates), and then as I moved in I could hear the noise of heavy firing from the town of Vitez. I could also see smoke rising from the centre of the town. As I moved in, I stopped in the area of the catholic church, which is located here. (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you mark that point "P1"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court exactly what you saw, as best you can recollect? I know these events are now some years old.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a number of things, and they are in no particular order, it was taking the panoramic view in. Starting from the left-hand side of the road as I am facing north, the first thing that I noticed were a number of houses on fire. I remember there being a house on fire behind me and to my left, and then further up the road, just slightly in front of me, on the left-hand side, there was a pavement area in front of a house, and there was a body of a dead civilian, a male of about 50 years old. It appeared that he had been shot in the head. He was lying on the side of the road, on the pavement area. I could see fighting or firing going on down the road. And then, running around to the right-hand side, although a number of the houses were on fire, I remember two specifically, and they were just on the right of where my vehicle was standing, my Warrior was standing. Then the right of those two houses, I looked through the front window and the house that was on fire, there were two bodies in the house and they were sitting, it appeared to be, at a table or a sort of table area, and they were on fire as well, and I remember reporting this on the radio back to our base location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the technical staff could bring up a previously admitted exhibit, which is exhibit 100/4, Z1/232, do you recognise that image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is basically exactly where I had stopped my vehicle and that was the body that I described on the left-hand side of the road and opposite to that, on the other side of the road, would have been the houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said, Captain Ellis, that there was an awful lot of firing going on. Could you distinguish the types of firing that you could hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could discern small arms fire, automatic rifle fire and repetition rifle fire; also a heavier calibre weapon I could hear operating down the road, possibly a heavy machine gun, and I could also hear either mortar rounds being detonated or mortar rounds being fired from further up the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at this point you decided to proceed off the main road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. On my right, and it is quite clear on the map, there is a road that runs down to the right past the church, which I will indicate now (indicates). As I was sitting there, a large amount of firing happened behind the houses which were forward and to my right. There was a lot of small arms firing and it was very big in its intensity. I presumed there would have been in that area. My intention was to take my vehicle down that side road to try to get around to the back of those houses, to try to locate the source of that firing, and so I took a right turn and I went to move down the road, leaving my other vehicle on the main road to cover my approach up there. As I moved down, there was a flat bed van, the cab had a flat wooden base to it, actually blocking the road, or blocking my access down that road. It was parked at a slight angle and on the back of that vehicle was a multi-barrelled anti-aircraft weapon of about 20 millimetre calibre, and it was stopped and unmanned on that road. There was a small gap on the right-hand side which I tried to manoeuvre my vehicle down and past. As I actually came up to the vehicle, it became apparent that I was not able to get past the vehicle on the road and so I started to try and push the vehicle off so I could move down. As this happened, a group of about four, possibly five HVO soldiers came out from the left-hand side of the access road. On the access road, there is a line of fences running down, wooden fences and I remember these soldiers came through like a side entrance to the houses that are located there (indicates). They were very hostile towards me and they made it apparent, with the gestures of both their weapons and their voices, that they were not happy with me firstly nudging this vehicle to try to get past it and secondly, it appeared that their intent was to actually stop me from running down the road as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, can you mark the point of this incident on the aerial photograph and mark it as "P2" and then if you take a seat. So that we can move quickly, Mr. Registrar, could the witness be shown exhibit 105, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the ELMO? Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a flat bed in the approximate position that it was parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the anti-aircraft weapon that was blocking your path down this side road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did this weapon look as if it had been firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember seeing empty cases, shell cases on the actual flat bed itself. However, I do not recall seeing empty cases in its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now return to the map itself, I think because you could not get past this anti-aircraft weapon you actually went back to the main road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I remember reporting this, because there were two of these weapons in the area, and our information cell was very interested in their whereabouts at those times. I reported the fact that a HVO flat bed was in the town of Vitez itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Had you seen that flat bed with that weapon anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had seen it on the main Zenica road that runs down -- there was a HVO rest area that they used to use. That is where I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you returned to the main road. Did you proceed on into the town itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I moved up the main road. Just to indicate that, I moved up from this position here and then I moved up to this area here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did anything occur at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did, yes. My initial intention for going up here was to try to actually move down this road here. However, as I got to this point here, I stopped my vehicle. The reason I stopped it is that a BiH soldier had run out from the houses on the right-hand side of the road. He was very young, approximately 17 or 18, and very frightened, and he was indicating that Muslims in the town needed help and that the HVO had attacked in the town and, having looked further through him, there was a line on pavement level, sort of basement-type flats and windows that I could see through at pavement level, and I remember seeing a line of frightened faces, civilian faces, women and children, and this man was trying to indicate that these were at risk. So I reported this back to my headquarters, and I would like to make a point here that initially, at this point, because of my conversation at the garage with the commander, I had actually had no reason to believe that it was not the HVO being attacked. However, as I moved around and the incidents that had happened up until this point, I remember at this point changing my mind, and that was significant as such that I actually reported it back, that the HVO were mounting an attack in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you mark this point as "P3", and for the purposes of the transcript, P3 is where you saw the young frightened Muslim soldier shouting "HVO, HVO" and where you saw the civilians through a basement window.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying now you attempted to turn right again down another side road, and if you could indicate that road to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I moved down this road here (indicates), and I remember coming to this cross-roads here and being engaged by small arms fire. At this point I actually had my head out of the turret because it gave a better panoramic view and I remember feeling the bullets go past me and hitting the side of the turret. I got down and then I pushed further on past the junction to move out of the danger area, again trying to get to a point here where I might be in a position to either sweep round and have a look or basically see what was going on on that side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, can you mark this point as "P4", where you were engaged by machine gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have indicated that with a line to the point where you were located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped here and then I moved up --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I move towards the witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just would like to express a concern that these markings, particularly in the black area of the photo, are not legible. They are going to be very difficult to figure out in the weeks and months to come after the witness leaves us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Try to use another system of marking, so that we can use those markings later on more effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you just mark over these marks? We will do it afterwards, in front of counsel, but for P4, the mark that you have just made, can you just try and make it much more clear. Could you mark over it again with the pen? The others will do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could draw the line. Fine, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Having been engaged here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should like to take advantage of this occasion to ask whether all the other maps with markings, either of the Defence or the Prosecution, whether these marks will remain, and the Registrar has just told me that there will be difficulty in photocopying them, so what the judges are asking is to have access to these documents later on. I do not have any practical solution to propose. The incident is closed, so please continue, Captain, answering the questions of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to recall your testimony, at P4, this is where you were engaged by machine gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was engaged by small arms fire here. I actually believe it to be automatic rifle fire. And then I moved up to a point here, at the end of the road, and that is actually where I stopped. As I stopped there, I was engaged by a medium machine gun, and obviously I started looking through my gunsight to see if I could identify the firing point. My gunner and I believed that the point of fire was coming from an area over this way (indicates), and as such we directed most of our looking in that area there. It was whilst looking for this machine gun that was engaging us that I noticed a large amount of troop movement through my gunsight, and it appeared that casualties were being moved into a building, or out of a building, or generally around a building, and that would have been in a line with where I was, and so in a line up to there (indicates). My memory fails me as to exactly the point now that I reported that troop movement being, although I did report it on a grid --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you say a grid, you mean a map reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A map reference, I gave a pinpoint map reference to that troop movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at this point you then turned your vehicle around and went back to the main road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We could not discern where the firing point was and we could not get any further information, so I turned my vehicle around and moved back to the main road. Then I pushed up the main road, where I could hear a lot of heavy firing happening and there was also a large amount of heavy machine gunfire from that area and it seemed like a new outbreak had taken place. So I moved up here (indicates) and stopped at around --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved up to here and I stopped at approximately that area there (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, if you can mark it as best you can "P5", and I suggest you use the red pen, because that appears to make a mark that is more discernible. What did you see at this particular point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped there and I saw two things of interest that stick out in my mind. The first one was that located approximately 50 metres up the road to my position there was a heavy calibre anti-aircraft weapon firing in the ground roll, directly into a red bricked building on the far side of the junction ahead of me on the right-hand side of the road, and it struck me as being strange that this weapon was actually sustaining fire into this building. There did not appear to be any reason for firing into it, there was no firing back from the building, there was no visible Defence. I reported the fact that there was a heavy calibre weapon firing into this building. I then looked to my left-hand side, because there was a lot of firing happening. At that part of the town of Vitez there is a depth of buildings on the left-hand side of the road, there is more than just the buildings lining the side, and as I looked down and to my left, I saw two groups of HVO soldiers moving down from north to south, so moving from that direction down (indicates). They seemed to be conducting house clearing. One of the groups appeared to have come out of a house and was firing at another house, the next one down, and the other group was making its way as a blob down to the next house down the road. It was at this point that I decided to leave the area. One of the groups was carrying a modern, very modern piece of equipment which I had not expected to see in the area at all. It was something I had not seen before. It was a modern anti-tank weapon that was quite capable of destroying my vehicle. There was no indication that they were about to use it against me; however, because of the situation and the fact we had been engaged previously I decided to extract both my vehicles back down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just to recall quickly, the anti-aircraft weapon that you had seen firing into a house, at what range was it firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapon was mounted approximately 50 metres on the other side of the road to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What is the normal range of a weapon like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are designed specifically for air defence. You can expect to hit targets accurately up to about 5.5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So its destructive force at 50 metres is absolutely enormous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What sort of damage would a weapon like that do to housing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firing high explosive rounds, the first one would impact and explode and destroy brickwork. The second one, when firing automatic, would probably go through the same hole that had been made and impact on the inside of the building, creating destruction on the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did there appear to be any defence coming from this building? Was there anybody firing back at this anti-aircraft weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that I can remember. I remember thinking it strange that a weapon of this nature was firing so heavily into this building, firstly because there was no real visible signs of defence and secondly because ammunition for these particular weapons was short in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The soldiers that you saw, and you say they were clearing houses, did you see any defence coming from those houses? Were these soldiers taking cover, was there any shooting at the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, in that entire time that you spent in Vitez, did you see any defence against the action that was going on at all, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can recall no defence, no co-ordinated action against HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You can take a seat now, Captain Ellis. What I suggest, Mr. President, as far as the markings are concerned, in the break Mr. Hayman and I can stand there together with the witness and ensure they are made as clear as possible so we do not waste any time of the court. You stated, Captain Ellis, that after sighting this anti-tank weapon obviously you were concerned it would place you and your crews at risk, so am I right in saying you then returned to the British battalion camp at Stari Bila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I returned to refuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there you spoke to the watch keeper and explained what had happened, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the operation that you have just seen in Vitez, did you make any estimation about the amount of ammunition that had been used by the HVO to actually conduct this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an enormous amount of ammunition fired, a lot more than I had seen. The only comparable action was in a large-scale conflict between the Bosnian Serbs right up in the north east of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was ammunition in short supply in Central Bosnia amongst the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And here there was plenty of ammunition to be fired, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you think when you saw that level of ammunition expenditure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that to achieve that amount of ammunition in a particular area -- that must have been an orchestrated move to actually gather ammunition into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at about midday of that day you actually went to the village of Ahmici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If now I could ask the Registrar to place exhibit 50D, please, which is the photographic copy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone, because the booths have a lot of trouble hearing him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, could you move the microphones towards you? Captain Ellis, why did you go to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were reports that a casualty had been discovered by one of the 9th 12th Lancer call signs. They were the reconnaissance squadron attached to us. They did not have the ability to evacuate her because of the nature of their vehicles and I was to escort an armoured ambulance to the village to pick the casualty up and take her to Travnik hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you arrived in Ahmici, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My initial impression, it was not just Ahmici, it was the Santici area as well, which lies south of Ahmici. There were a lot of houses on fire, there was a lot of destruction, and the one thing that I did notice was the fact that the mosque minaret had been brought to the ground and the mosque itself had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you actually discover this female casualty in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved up into the village of Ahmici, I will just indicate on the map. Can you hear in the booths if I speak here? Can I move the microphone over? Is that better? I moved up the main Ahmici road, which runs here, and I met the reconnaissance call sign here and then we moved up this road here to an area approximately there, just before the upper mosque (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you discover when you arrived at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whilst I was there there was a casualty on the floor, she was on the left-hand side of the road. It was a woman that had been shot. The cavalry call sign that was there, the reconnaissance call sign, had administered first aid to her. She was not in a very good way and I remember her husband was there as well at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you give a more precise description of her injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe she had actually been shot in the head and in the legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You evacuated her to Travnik hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know if she was a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By her garb, I believe her to have been a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you give a brief but broader description of the damage to the village of Ahmici that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, there were a number of houses in the Ahmici and Santici area, Santici being the area there (indicates), south of Ahmici. There were a number of houses on fire and a number of the houses had a lot of bullet pock marks in the actual outer walls of the buildings. They were evidence of RPG, rocket-propelled grenade strikes against walls and there were a few cases of the petal shape that a mortar round would form, causing shrapnel damage to buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say that the mosque had indeed been destroyed and indeed the court has seen photographic evidence of this, so I am not going to show that again, but do you remember at the time forming an opinion about how the minaret had been brought down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes. The minaret itself, looking at its structure, was a very solid building, it was concrete with reinforced steel, and I formed two possible solutions as to how it had been destroyed. The first one was that a reasonably heavy piece of artillery could have engaged it at point blank range. I believe this not to have been the case, because firstly I do not believe there was any artillery in the area capable of achieving damage such as that; secondly, they would have had to hit it, and thirdly, the possible secondary danger to the actual gun crew themselves would have basically meant that firing would have been impractical. So I am of the opinion that the mosque was deliberately blown down by placed explosive charges, and it would be in much the same way as you would actually blow a tree down with explosives. You would place a necklace of explosives round the tree or you would bore holes into the tree and place explosives inside. When you blew up the tree it would be lifted up, severed, and sat down. The damage to the mosque when you look at the photographs is the same as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any livestock in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was livestock, it was dead though.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A lot of dead livestock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember seeing two dogs and a cow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think if we can now move to the next day, 17th April, in the early morning you went to Vitez or you returned to the town of Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you see and hear in the town of Vitez that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fires in the buildings themselves had burnt down somewhat, they were still smouldering. It was relatively calm and peaceful, there was the occasional burst of small arms fire, but there was nothing of major interest within the town. However I do recall the sky line around the town; looking both to the left and to the right, I could see burning houses illuminating the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that after your return to the town of Vitez you took the road out towards Ahmici and Santici and that your attention was drawn to a flash of colour on the side of the road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you actually preceded up a side road, which if you could just indicate on the aerial photograph, if you can remember the approximate area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was this road here, very early in the morning (indicates). It was light. I pushed down this road and moved up that road there. I cannot remember the exact location of the buildings, but I believe it to have been one of these three here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you proceeded left off a side road on the Ahmici Santici road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to the left of the main road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you find when you came to a halt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a house firstly with the front door open that led inside the house. Forward of that, there was a path and then a hedge and then an open field and about ten metres from the open field, there were two bodies. There was a body of a woman, approximately 40 years old and she was appearing to hold on to the body of a child which was about 5, possibly 6 years old. I looked at them, and then I started to look around the area in more detail and I saw a body of a man about 40, maybe 50 years old, in civilian clothes, dead on the hedge line of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any sign of damage to the house itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were pock marks on the wall, but there was no fire damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did your soldiers form an opinion as to what had happened at this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The opinion that myself and my soldiers formed, bearing in mind we had seen a lot of damage over the last 24 hours or so, was that this was a family that had been running away from a house and had been shot down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As best you can, can you mark this location on the map using the red marker? This will be P6 for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will check with Mr. Hayman in the break to see that he can clearly see it. I think this is very early in the morning that this sighting occurred. Do you remember approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 6.30 or 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, am I right in saying, that at about 6.45 in the morning you moved on to the village of Sivrino Selo, because you had been informed of another casualty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I wonder if you can just flip the aerial photographs over, if that is possible, if the usher could assist, because we need to refer to the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the usher could.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am sorry to have to make the court staff perform acrobatics in order to deal with the exhibits. I will try and move more quickly. Can you just indicate on the map the location of Sivrino Selo and the location of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez itself is here and Sivrino Selo is here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying you had been informed of a casualty at this location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I had been asked to move up and locate a casualty that had been identified in the area and I was to take him to Travnik hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you find when you arrived in Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved up the track from the Santici Ahmici area and moved into the village itself. When I arrived there was a farm complex on the right-hand side, and at that farm complex there was a family there, about four or five people, and there was a boy of about 14 years old. He was lying on the floor, and he had been shot in the legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the state of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very frightened. As far as I was aware -- they were civilians, they were dressed in civilian clothes, and they were very frightened, they were very scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did they identify themselves to you as Muslims, or as Croats? Were you aware at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could show to you exhibits 106 and 107, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. This actually coupled with the other photograph of the small grey building. If you are looking on the road at the right-hand side, that would be the courtyard that was formed on the right. That building there was the main farm building on the left, and then at the end of the courtyard was that building there (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these photographs should be looked at together. Captain Ellis, are these the two buildings where you collected the child from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, yes. However, they were not in that state when I was there, they were whole buildings, complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did they look like when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had no real collateral damage at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will make it clear for the purposes of the transcript and for my learned friend Mr. Hayman, these were photographs that were taken by the Office of the Prosecutor, by Mr. Simon Leach, I think, in 1996, so that is just to make that absolutely clear. So these buildings were in perfect order when you went to Sivrino Selo, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could apply, with the caveat I have given, for the admission of these photographs 106 and 107 into evidence, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection, of course, reserving our previously stated position with respect to these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. What is the number, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the usher could assist again with the exhibits, we now need exhibit 56, which is the aerial photograph. Now if we can move ahead to the next day, which is 18th April 1993, in the very early hours of that morning I think you were told by your battalion to rendezvous with a group of Muslim refugees at a factory near to Vitez, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The instruction that I had received was that there were a group of approximately 200 refugees in the area of the factory to the west of Vitez, and that there were also some coaches in the area that were to take them to the refugee centre. They had not been able to meet with each other and I was to locate both groups, marry them up and then move them on to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the map the location of this factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The factory complex is here (indicates). It was very difficult to actually find on the map itself though because it is not actually on the map because it is a defence installation from previous years. So the route that I took to find it was to move up this road here to the actual main factory entrance there (indicates). My initial thoughts were to try and move into the factory to see if the refugees had located themselves there. As I got to the gate itself, there was an old sentry post on the right-hand side and a pull up/pull down barrier across the road that was down. At the time I was actually closed down, which means that my hatch was closed on my vehicle to afford better protection. At night-time, I was not wanting to put my head up, and for this reason, we were using night sights, which gives a very restricted field of vision. I remember moving up to the gate itself, and there was one HVO soldier on the gate, who upon my arrival ran out and started gesturing with his weapon that I was not to go through the gate and so I put my head out of my vehicle. The man was very aggressive, very hostile towards me, and I was not really aware of the situation within the factory itself. Everything I had seen led me to believe that the civilians that are supposed to be meeting could have been in danger in the factory by the nature of this soldier's actions so I got back down into my vehicle and pushed through the gate itself to see if I could actually look for the refugees in the factory complex. I moved into the factory complex and I could not find any, so I turned around, moved out again, and then I moved along this road here (indicates). This took me up to a road that went up to the area here, and the reason that I decided to move up to this area was that I could see a number of houses burning against the skyline . I moved up the road to this village. It would have been one of these two and I moved into the village centre itself from the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, what was the name of the village that you entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Donje Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, could you describe the night sky generally that night, what you and your soldiers could see on the horizon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically on the western side of Vitez, it was night-time and wherever you looked you could make out the pinpoints of fires burning against the night sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you got to the village of Donje Veceriska, which you have indicated on the aerial photograph, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the time I actually moved into the village, it was dawn and light had broken. I moved into the village from the northern side and when I arrived I found a group of approximately 100 plus civilian refugees standing in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the state of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilians, they were very frightened and I remember that one girl came out from the right-hand side of the crowd. She was about 17 or 18 and she spoke very good English and I got out of my vehicle and I went down to speak to her and I asked her why they were standing there, what the matter was. She said that some soldiers had come to the village, they had shot some of the people, and they had told them to get out of the village and if they were not gone very soon, then they would come back and kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did she identify the soldiers that had done this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said they were HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the people in the village, to which ethnic group did they belong, did you work that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were there any injured people amongst these civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked to provide first aid to some wounded people that had been shot. I was taken into a house, just to the right-hand side of the road, where there were two people. The first one was a young man of about 18 years of age, and the second one was a woman of about 50 years of age. The man was in civilian clothes, the woman was wearing Muslim garb.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the injuries of these two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man had been shot in the chest, the entrance wound was on his chest side and the exit wound was on his back. There was a lot of damage to his back, and I believe that he was not going to live very long. We carried out some very basic first aid and we put him into the back of our vehicle. The woman had been shot in the legs three or four times, and we gave her morphine, we attended to her injuries, and then again put her in the back of my vehicle with the intent to move them to Travnik hospital. I remember radioing back to our base location, explaining the situation on the radio, requesting a further patrol to move up and attend to these people, because they were frantic that I was to take them with them, but I had no means of doing so. I was told that I was not to stay there and I was to move these civilian casualties to Travnik hospital. So I remember, very reluctantly, I moved off to Travnik. I was followed by about three or four cars packed full of people into Travnik, and I left the remainder of these people in the village, although I subsequently understand that another patrol came out and actually met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think after this point you actually returned to the village of Sivrino Selo, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you indicate again on the large map the location of Vitez and the location of Sivrino Selo? If you could do that slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez is here (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you look to the east of Vitez, slightly more, you will see Sivrino Selo, to the east of the Zenica mountain road, a distance of approximately two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think this is where you had earlier rescued the little boy from the farm complex, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you returned there. What did you observe when you returned to the village of Sivrino Selo on 18th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly there was some collateral damage by small arms to the houses themselves, and I also heard a large bang, possibly a mortar round exploding, about 600 metres to the north of my position, on the northern end of the village. I was coming in from the east so it would have been above me on the hillside. I reported the fact that there was mortar fire in the area, and I left one of my call signs at a junction about 300 or 400 metres away from the position where I picked the boy up. I picked the boy up basically in the centre of the village. It was at this location that I actually stopped and I reported my position. When I was there, a group of about two or three Muslim men ran out, wearing civilian clothes, and they were very frightened indeed. They were indicating that something was happening, and I remember looking forward and about 200 or 300 metres on the hillside, there was a line of houses, and the first house on the right-hand side suddenly -- there was a large explosion on its frontage, which created a lot of dust. It did not completely destroy the house, but it was obviously a major hit on the construction of it. I initially thought that it was a mortar round that had hit the house, because of the bang I had heard earlier. About five minutes later, the next house, suddenly a large explosion on its frontage, and the same sort of thing. It was at this point that I believe that it was not a mortar firing. For information, a mortar can be fired at an area 100 metres square. Where the round lands in that area, it cannot be selective. Therefore because two houses had been hit, subsequently to each other, I believed that it was not a mortar firing. I remember trying to look for a firing point of whatever weapon system was firing at me, and I pulled the civilians round to the back of my vehicle and I remember getting out of my turret with a map and I offered them the map, which is similar to the one that the court can see, and asked them to indicate to me where it was that that was firing at us from, and they could not do it, they could not read the map. The next thing I did was offered them a piece of paper and a pencil, in an attempt to get them to draw me what was firing at us, so I knew what it was. They drew something which resembled a mortar, but it was not a particularly good picture, so again I did not have any indication of what it was that was firing at us. I then got back into the turret to carry on looking. As I did so, there was a huge rushing of air noise, a massive whoosh, and I could feel the air being sucked out around me. There was a split second silence, and a tree about five or six metres up the road from me was hit by something. I initially thought I was being engaged by a tank. I still could not see where the firing point was and I ordered my driver to reverse very quickly back down the road and I threw the two people into the back of my vehicle as I did so. As we reversed, another round landed exactly at the point that I had been at. At this point, I believed I was being engaged by a heavy anti-armour weapon of some description. When we stopped again, my gunner said that he could identify the firing point, and I asked him to give me a target indication as to where the firing point was, to which he did, and I still could not identify myself. Our rules of engagement in Central Bosnia were such that if you could not identify the firing point actually firing then you were not allowed to engage, and so I did not engage on my gunner's say-so that he had seen something, because he could have been mistaken. It was at this point that I saw some movement and I identified the firing point as well, and what was happening was that they were moving the piece of equipment, which I identified as a recoilless gun, into the back of a small light green car. They drove it into what appeared to be a school building. I looked at my map and the only school actually that I could see on the map, because I was rushing things, was the school actually in Ahmici and I gave that as the grid. With hindsight, I know that to be the wrong grid and I was being engaged from the area of the school in Dubravica, and the reason that I know that I was is that I went up there subsequently with Colonel Bob Stewart, who was my commanding officer at the time, to go and negotiate a prisoner release some two days further on and I identified the building as the building I had seen from my gunsight. I can now say that I was engaged from the school at Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This recoilless gun, if those shells had hit your vehicle, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The usual calibre of weapon of this nature is 100 millimetre, which would have been enough to destroy my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are moving to 11.25, I can finish within two minutes, or I can pause now. There is only one other incident. I will be very quick about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, please, if you can hurry it up and finish with the last incident and remind him of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think after this incident happened, I would just like to clarify one point with you; did you see any soldiers in Sivrino Selo at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was there any resistance of any sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think at this time you felt the force of an absolutely massive explosion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my vehicle we had stopped, we had seen the green car disappear, and I remember feeling this big force of, this shock wave hit me, at the same time a huge bang, a massive explosion. I looked down to where the bang had come from and there was a huge plume of smoke rising from the town of Vitez. I remember at the time we had a patrol in the town who reported that there had been a massive explosion, there were a large amount of casualties and they needed call signs in the town as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far were you from Vitez at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was about two kilometres, again in the village of Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You went into Vitez. What did you find when you got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved into Vitez, I was not the first call sign there, there were already vehicles in the area, there was a scene of complete chaos, civilians running round in complete hysteria, there were civilian casualties and there was complete devastation to the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could ask the technical staff to bring up Z1/246, which is 100/8, previously admitted by Major Thomas, do you recognise that image, Captain Ellis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the town of Vitez following the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the local civilians were literally scrambling on to your vehicles in order to get out of the area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were, yes. They were running from most directions to where the centre of our vehicles were. We were trying to marshall them with our soldiers who were on the ground. I remember getting out the back of my vehicle, shouting at Colonel Martyn Thomas where he wanted me to take these people and he shouted at me Travnik, so we threw as many people as we could in the back of my two vehicles and then moved them to the hospital at Travnik, and my army chaplain was there trying to organise some sort of reception for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The composition of this group of people, mainly men, mainly women, or children or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were killed or injured as a result of that bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number. I know there were a lot of injuries and a lot of deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you recall how many people were taken to Travnik from Vitez on that day by the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I do not know the exact number. I personally took about 15 to 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The final question from this part of your testimony; what was your feeling at the time about the purpose of that explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see no tactical reason why that explosion had taken place, and there was just one of shock, that something like that could have happened in what was really a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, if you wish to break there, I have possibly another 15 minutes of questioning after the break and then I will have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We are going to break and resume in 20 minutes at 11.50. (11.30 am) (A short break) (11.50 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Captain Ellis, if we can now just conclude your examination-in-chief with the other significant offence that occurred in your time there, am I right in saying that on 19th April you were tasked to meet a Red Cross convoy going to Zenica from Jelinak, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you could stand and just indicate with your pointer exactly what occurred on that particular day, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I moved down the main road here (indicates), with the intention of going to the junction there, to RV with an ICRC convoy. What happened is that as I was in the area of Travnik, which is here (indicates), there was a very large articulated truck blocking the road. It had large tree logs on its back, to add it some weight, and it was blocking the road totally. I tried to push the truck out of the road with my vehicle, but it was too heavy for my vehicle to move and I had to actually get to my rendezvous for the convoy and so I moved up and moved back to that junction there (indicates) and then I took a northern route through the village of Loncari and then my intention was to move up to Jelinak and down through Putis and then on to the road again, circumventing the actual truck that was in the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As you proceeded what did you perceive was actually happening in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I moved up, I got to the area of Loncari, which is about a kilometre short of the village of Jelinak, and from that point, I could see a large battle taking place around Jelinak itself. There was artillery fire falling around the area of the village, and there was also -- I could hear heavy fighting being conducted. If I looked through my gunsight, I could see very small figures running around in the village itself. Also on my right-hand side, there was a hill running up to a high point which you can actually make out on the map. Moving down in an organised fashion south from the village of Jelinak were HVO forces and they were basically retreating from Jelinak. I remember as well that there were three people actually on the road that I was on -- two people carrying a casualty back down, and they were moving down towards Loncari and then beyond that as well. I pushed forward with my vehicle, still intending to move through, but the fighting was very, very intense in Jelinak and I did not want to move into the village itself, because I felt it could possibly put my troops at risk. So I identified a very small track and I took a route which took me 400 metres to the south of Jelinak, put me back on to the Putis road and then I went back down to the main road and met up with the convoy again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These were HVO soldiers that you saw withdrawing, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think as opposed to Vitez, what you had seen in Vitez, this was actually a military engagement between two different forces, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The impression that we had formed at the time -- this is with the benefit of speaking to other people that I was working with -- was that the HVO had initially launched an offensive, the BiH had turned the tide and they were actually fighting and retaking ground which had been taken by the HVO. What I believe I witnessed here was the Muslim forces, the BiH, retaking the village of Jelinak from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think on 27th April, if we can move ahead now in time, you were returning from the city of Zenica, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you passed by again the village of Sivrino Selo, which you have referred to earlier in your testimony, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was moving on the mountain road from Zenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map the route that you were taking and the location of Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mountain road is this red road here that runs south from Zenica down towards Vitez. It is this area here, slightly north from the Sivrino Selo junction (indicates). This is where I was on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court what happened at Sivrino Selo when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got to a point in the road where there is a cluster of houses on the right-hand side and there were two large groups of people, possibly between 80 and 100 people, hiding behind these houses. They were very frightened. I had recognised the man who was the father of the 14 year old that I had taken to hospital some week or so earlier, and so I stopped my vehicle and I got out of my vehicle and I went down to speak to the man that I recognised. He recognised me. The product of the conversation was that the HVO had moved into Sivrino Selo and attacked the village and they had instructed everyone to get out of the village, or they would be killed. There were groupings -- the people that were there were the people from the village of Sivrino Selo and upwards to Pirici. They were stuck there, and the reason they were stuck is because whenever they tried to move away from the cover of these houses, they were engaged by sniper fire from the eastern side of the road, and if you look at the map, that takes you down to the area of the Dubravica road. That was the area that I believed them to be being engaged from. We firstly tried to identify the firing point, but we could not, and it did become obvious that they were being sniped at, because whenever anyone stepped out, including my soldiers, from behind either my vehicles or the houses, we were shot at with deliberate single shots. So what I did was I moved my vehicles together to form a shield, instructed everyone to move around to the left-hand side of my vehicles, and then we moved south down the road to move them away from the area. When I was driving down the road, we got to a point in the road that provides cover from view, because of rockiness on either side, and the liaison officer, Captain Matthew Douglas Whatley, was moving up the road from the other direction in a Land Rover. He stopped, I got out of my vehicle, explained the situation, and he took the people from there. I drove off. I cannot remember what task I was on and I have to admit, I do not remember the fate of those people or what Captain Douglas Whatley sorted out for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were these civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Men, women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a mixture of men, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were they Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You formed an armoured wall and the people hid behind your vehicles in order to protect them from sniper fire as they walked down the road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think we can now moved ahead in time to May 1st. You actually went to the village of Jelinak where you had previously seen this battle taking place, where you thought at the time that the Bosnian army were retaking this village, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What did you find when you got to the village of Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went up to Jelinak with Colonel Bob Stewart, and it was there that a rendezvous had been arranged with General Morien, who was the commander of the UN forces. What we did was to move into the village and the first thing I remember hitting me was the smell of death and decay. I moved into the village, we parked our vehicles up, we were purely there to provide an escort for Colonel Stewart whilst he met up with Morien. I got out of my vehicle and there were BiH soldiers sitting around. I went up and I spoke to the soldiers with the aid of an interpreter that was there with us. The crux of the conversation was that the HVO had taken the village in the weeks previous to this and that the BiH had retaken the village and the one impression that I got, having spoken to the soldiers, was that they were particularly angry with the HVO because as far as they were concerned the HVO moved in and butchered their families and their civilian friends. They were out there and they were very angry with the whole situation. They took me to show me some things that they said had been carried out by the HVO, and there were two old fires that were completely burnt out, the ashes were cold, and on top of one fire there was half a body, a torso of a body, that was -- it was burnt, it was browned, it had been roasted over this fire, it was in a state of decay, and then to the right of that, there was another fire and in that fire, or in the remains the fire, there were a pair of boots, and the boots, remarkably, had been untouched by the flames; but sticking out of these boots were -- the burnt flesh was still in the boots and there were just two leg bones sticking out. Then they showed me the house behind where these two remains were and I remember the house, it had a platform, like a veranda at more or less ground level. On the veranda there were bullet holes on the wall and there were bloodstains on the wall and on the floor. Although I did not actually go into the house, I was not involved in any clearance of bodies from the area, I am aware that my platoon sergeant, Sergeant Kujivinsky was, and obviously I had a very close working relationship with my sergeant and I talked to him in great detail about things. It was the same house that he had to go and collect bodies from that had been tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he say to you whether these bodies that were recovered, whether they were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were civilian bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did he say these people had been butchered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said they had been tortured. I am not aware in what way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many people were in the basement of this house? How many dead bodies were recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Moving on almost finally to the subject of body clearance, I know that the Cheshire Regiment was involved in this rather grisly task that had to be done. Was your platoon involved in the clearance of civilian bodies during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were involved in one particular clearance that sticks out in my mind generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was quite well publicised. There was a particular house in the village of upper Ahmici that a family had been found of five or six bodies, a young child and some other bodies that were unrecognisable, and it was my platoon's task to move up there with Colonel Stewart, who was personally in charge of the clearance operation, and my platoon moved out the remains from that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was the regiment involved generally in the activity of body clearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The regiment was not, it was specifically my company, which included another two platoons, 1 platoon and 2 platoon that were involved in the clearance of bodies from Vitez and the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many civilian bodies were recovered from these areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there were 96 bodies recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said in Ahmici that the bodies were unrecognisable. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they had been burnt beyond recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you mentioned to me that many of your soldiers were affected deeply by this exercise, and I wonder if you could briefly explain to the court how people reacted to the sight of all of these dead civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general feeling of the whole area, and it was brought out at the body clearance at Ahmici, from the platoon and from the troops as a whole, was one of sheer disgust, and I know that it affected the married men in my platoon a lot more than the single men amongst us. I believe the reason for it, and a close friend of mine who is now a sergeant in the army, who was part of my platoon, who I speak to, the reason that the married people were more affected is because they could relate far more to what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it not the case that almost two years later somebody broke down in your office because of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Captain Ellis, have you ever met General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to 20 times, 15 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You were a very junior officer at the time, so you were not involved in any liaison activities. Why did you have occasion to meet General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tasking that we were given and it was before the April 16th period and in the month preceding it. We ran a sort of armoured taxi service between locations within our area to provide a protection for commanders to take them to various meetings that were being organised for them to try to create a solution to the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say an armoured taxi service; specifically, to which locations did you take General Blaskic and where did you collect him from? Just as you can remember, as best you can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three main areas that we conducted our operations in, and the first one was in Vitez itself. Within Vitez, I sometimes had occasion to pick him up from the British battalion base at the school, and then take him onwards, either to the school -- the Hotel Vitez in the town of Vitez itself and then the other two places were in Busovaca and in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many times did you take him to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I specifically remember three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever collect him in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So when you collected him in Kiseljak, he had made his own way there or in fact had been taken by another platoon of the battalion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that he would have already been there. I do not know how he got there. I was responsible for picking him up from there and taking him back to, nine times out of ten, to the Vitez school, the British battalion base.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say you were involved in this activity 15 to 20 times. Were there other platoons in the battalion that were also operating this armoured taxi service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There would only ever be one task of this, at most one per day. In my company, there were another two platoons, within the British battalion base, there were another three platoons that could have conducted these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the time period in which you were operating this taxi service to these locations you have specified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mid February through to March and then running up to when everything happened in April time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Was he accompanied by individuals when he travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I remember that the taskings that we were given were actually formal taskings on tasking sheets. Usually the task was to pick up Blaskic plus one. Usually when we arrived at whatever location, and it was only when it happened away from the school, was that there would be too many people to fit into our vehicles. We had the capacity to lift ten people, and there were too many people to get in, and it got to the point where I refused to take anyone else other than himself and the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So General Blaskic plus one other individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at a point -- sometimes I took more when we first started conducting these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These individuals around him, do you know what function -- what was your feeling at the time as to what function these people had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was of the impression that the majority of them were bodyguards of some description. However, at some point, there were one or two that were able to talk to him on a more work-like level and not as purely orders to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these would have been staff officers, is that your feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that was only on a few occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you described these people to me; what was your description of the manner of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever we picked anyone up, from bodyguard up to Blaskic, they were hostile, aggressive and unfriendly to us. They were very arrogant and the sort of bodyguard grouping were particularly nasty individuals. They were equipped better as well, in their small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What were they dressed in? What uniform were they dressed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the time it was black garb. The bodyguards tended to wear black bomber jackets, on the HVO badges that they wore, there was a lot more gold than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How was General Blaskic dressed at this time when you saw him on all these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the time he was dressed in black. However, there were times when he would have a DPM, disruptive pattern material, camouflage-type smock over the top of whatever he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How did the soldiers feel about operating this taxi service, your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of us -- and this is talking not just of my platoon sergeants, but soldiers out of my platoon and within other companies -- we felt it was a waste of our time, an unnecessary task, and the general feeling was that we were being used for a task that we should not have been used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to transport a Bosnian army commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not, although I do know that other platoons did transport Bosnian army commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One final area of questioning: what communications systems did the British battalion have in their Warrior vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every section vehicle, that is every vehicle that was out there, had a VHF radio set, very high frequency radio set, and each command vehicle, and basically mine would be the lowest vehicle that would be equipped, would have a HF, high frequency, radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: From your practical experience from operating in the Lasva Valley, what was the range of your VHF radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended totally on the conditions and the location that you were from. There were times when you could not speak to someone 500 metres down the road. There were other times when you could get communications a good 70 to 80 kilometres away. It depended where you were and what the weather was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It depended how well you knew the terrain as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were obviously places that you knew you could get communications with. Our signals platoon did conduct reconnaissance to find radio black spots. That is the point where you cannot maintain radio communications and obviously these areas were given to us and we tried to send radio communications from the areas that we knew we could get reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you ever manage to obtain VHF radio communications from Kiseljak to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
