utterances.text: One of them was a T-55?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Two of them were T-34s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You knew at the time or learned that they were part of the 341st Tank Brigade of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were the entire brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, strange as it sounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because having spoken and reported the incident to our information cell, he informed me, yes, that is the grouping known as that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you know, did you ever see the HVO in the Lasva Valley in possession of any tanks during your tour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the HVO, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On 1st May, you went back to Jelinak, or perhaps went into Jelinak for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With Colonel Stewart and General Morien?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I initially went with Colonel Stewart and General Morien arrived afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You had a conversation with certain BiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you what HVO forces or units were involved in the fighting in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember now whether they did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When they related these horrible events to you, did they say whether they had observed them or they had heard them second-hand from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any basis to verify from what you saw who exactly had done what to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The impression that I formed, and it was an impression, was that they were telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than your own abilities in that regard, general abilities, did you have any specific evidence or basis from which to determine who had actually done what to whom in Jelinak, in terms of the burned bodies and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I confirm dates? This was on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This was on 1st May when you went with Colonel Stewart and later met up with General Morien?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When did I initially go up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe on 19th April you went to the Loncari area and saw the retreating HVO troops carrying their wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from what I felt at the time, and that was that they were telling the truth. I had no other reason to think otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that your complete answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they were telling the truth. I cannot think of anything at the moment as to why I might change that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you cannot articulate any basis one way or the other, is that right, for being able to verify or not being able to verify exactly who had done what to whom in respect of the village of Jelinak with respect to burned bodies and other atrocities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not personally say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only point I am going to make is that the witness has already answered the question. He bases it on the fact that he thought these Bosnian soldiers were telling the truth; he cannot say anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is exact. Proceed please, Mr. Hayman, to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will. I agree he said that in his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described transporting Tihomir Blaskic from time to time up to mid April 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been around that time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In February, March and up to the middle of April 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it possibly could have been after, but I certainly did before that time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were the purpose of these transports to take him to meetings organised by international organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official reason for the purpose of these transports was, yes, to take Blaskic to meetings, to try and broker agreements amongst different factions. However, as I have also said, the feeling of the company as a whole, and it was not just myself, was that we were being used not just to take him to meetings, but I remember at least on one occasion when he requested that I drop him off at a place different to where I was supposed to have been taking him, and when I initially refused he got very angry and so I dropped him off where he had asked to be dropped off. The reason why he asked to get dropped off at a different place than I had been told to take him to, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it on the way, this other place? Was it on the way to the meeting that he was going to attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was, nine times out of ten, on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So, in other words, after he had attended a meeting in Busovaca or Kiseljak, he is coming back into Vitez, you might drop him in Busovaca instead of taking him back to Vitez, is that what you mean, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR keep a log or a record of whether they transported Tihomir Blaskic and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Who gave the orders for these transports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way that my company was organised was you had a company working operations and then you had a company off operations. The person heading up the operations as a whole for the battalion would have given direction to the company ops officer or second in command and then the way it worked was that whoever was on patrol that day used to pick up a tasking sheet to say "this is what you have to achieve this day". Who was responsible for producing that, I do not know. There was no record of those kept, it was purely a paper thing that we would throw away after our patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said some of the persons you transported at times were aggressive and unfriendly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You described one occasion when Tihomir Blaskic asked to be dropped in Busovaca instead of Kiseljak on the way back from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was taking him -- yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He was coming back from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was coming back from Vitez and I was due to take him to Kiseljak and he asked to be dropped in Busovaca, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other than that incident, was there any other incident where Tihomir Blaskic became aggressive towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say aggressive. He was surly, unfriendly, arrogant, every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have a substantive discussion with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I could not speak his language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I take it you, along with the other BritBat soldiers, resented having to perform this duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did it to the best of our ability, and sometimes it formed part of other taskings that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It formed a part of other taskings, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously the UN headquarters being in Kiseljak, we might have to pick the mail up, so we doubled it up with picking him up, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you out on patrol at all on either 14th or 15th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any activities on either 14th or 15th April 1993 that indicated preparatory steps for a large attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already stated that there was a period of tension, and that when it happened on the 16th, people did not fully realise the situation because people were not expecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand that answer, but I am asking a somewhat more direct question. On 14th or 15th April, did you see any activities on the part of the HVO or anyone else in the Vitez area that were in the nature of preparations for a large attack, military attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am going purely off memory here. Around the area of Vitez, I do not recall seeing any preparations being made. However, I believe that when I was involved with the HVO staff officers, which would have been I think, if my memory serves me correctly, a few days before the incidents that happened on the 16th -- could you verify that, whether I am right with my dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say the incident involving HVO staff officers, I do not know what you are referring to. I would be happy to show you your statement to the OTP if you would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was involved with a meeting between people to try to reach a resolution of that. I remember speaking about this earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If there is something that the Prosecutor has that would help you refresh your recollection, I invite him to chime in, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This is a somewhat foreign process for me, actually assisting in the examination, but I will do it because I do recall earlier the witness testifying about the kidnapping of four HVO staff officers, which he knew about, and which he was involved in the negotiation for their release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should like us to focus the question. We are going to have a break very soon. Mr. Hayman, do you have a lot more, that is my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have one or two more questions, then I suggest we break and then I have about five more minutes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, could I just finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we finish this one area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On this particular point, I should like you to repose your question. You started from the general context, whether before the 16th the witness expected an attack of this scope, and whether he participated in negotiations with the HVO. Was that the question, did he have that impression? Was that your question, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it, Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please, rephrase that question clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The kidnapping of the four staff officers in the Novi Travnik area I believe was on or about 14th April 1993 -- if that is of assistance, counsel can interject if they disagree. My question was, on the 14th or 15th, did you see any preparatory steps being taken in the Vitez area for a large military attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have previously stated, not in the Vitez area, but as I was in Novi Travnik, as a direct result of those kidnappings, there were large amounts of HVO troops in Novi Travnik and they were aggressive towards us. I would not say it was open hostility, but they were very unfriendly towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Anything else that you saw that would be responsive to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This would be a convenient break, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume in 20 minutes at 4.25. (4.05 pm) (A short break) (4.25 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First I would like to offer into evidence the transparency which was placed on top of exhibit 56, the aerial of the Vitez region. I think it has been taken down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Transparency over exhibit 56, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We would also like to offer the witness's prior statement to the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor, four pages in length, dated April 24th 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection? Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to the admission of the witness statement, but what the Prosecutor would like is the opportunity to review the statement that Mr. Hayman took from the witness, because we may wish to offer that into evidence ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am not offering it to them, your Honour, and I do not intend to give it to them unless the court would order me to do so, which I do not think there is a basis for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is a statement made to the Prosecution, therefore a priori it is a statement -- no, not made to the Prosecution? Maybe I am wrong, it is a statement by the witness made to the Defence, is that so, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could clarify on behalf of my learned friend and myself, there are two statements in existence. The first statement is a statement that was taken down by the Office of the Prosecutor in 1995, that is the statement that Mr. Hayman is offering into evidence. Subsequently, Mr. Hayman interviewed this witness on his own, and he took a statement from that witness, which he has referred to when he was cross-examining the witness. We are asking for sight of that statement because we may wish to actually offer that statement into evidence. There is no property in a witness, that is why Mr. Hayman was allowed to interview him in the first place, and we feel that it is perfectly legitimate for us to request sight of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would simply ask that the court request briefing on this question, if it is going to seriously entertain the issue. This issue has been ruled on by other Trial Chambers and statements of Defence witnesses have been found not to be producable, so if the court is going to entertain it, I would ask the court to ask briefing so it has a proper explanation and setting forth of the parties' positions before making any ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wish to consult my colleagues. (Pause). The Trial Chamber feels that this document was identified by the witness, therefore the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the whole document should be admitted into evidence, so as to allow the Prosecutor to respond to it. Therefore, Mr. Hayman, you will submit the whole statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to, Mr. President? The Prosecution statement or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is the question that I put a moment ago. We are referring to the statement that you, the Defence, took from the witness, the second statement, your statement, the statement that you collected from Captain Ellis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I never showed it to the witness, your Honour. He never identified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He identified, he agreed with the fact that -- you read the declaration to him when you interviewed him, did you not? It is not a synthesised document, it is not a summary, you had an interview with the witness and you took a statement from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I did not. It is not a statement in that nature. I tape recorded some of my interviews. I have a tape. It is not something he was ever shown, it was never read to him, he never reviewed it, he never signed anything; there is no statement in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps the terms were not properly explained to the Trial Chamber. I am going to consult my colleagues again. What were you implying, Mr. Cayley? You spoke of a statement and Mr. Hayman, you too spoke of a statement. That is what misled the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The statement taken by the Prosecutor's Office was signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right. But the statement that you took from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I did not take a statement. I tape recorded my interview with him, a tape which has never left my possession. It is my work product, it contains attorney/client privileged materials and I do not intend to surrender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But a moment ago, when you asked the witness to identify something, when you gave him sentences on the ELMO? This one, the statement that you drew a sentence from: "I could see quite a bit of fighting going on between the Muslims and the HVO." That is the Prosecutor's statement? Yes, all right. In that case, there is no debate. What is the statement that you wish to be admitted into evidence, Mr. Hayman? Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is what I understood from the beginning, Mr. Cayley. Therefore I see no objection to the admission of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection to the admission of that statement. However, in respect of the interview that took place between Mr. Hayman and Captain Ellis, Mr. Hayman referred in his cross-examination of the witness to the content of that interview, so the content, or part of the content, of that interview has been introduced into the court. He referred to it specifically. I recall, and I am sure he does as well, and the point that we are making is that if that is to take place the Prosecutor should have the right to review either the tape or a transcript of that interview that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is another problem that you are raising, that is another issue. I think that you wish to contest certain elements. You will have the right to re-examine the witness regarding what Mr. Hayman said when he cross-examined the witness. He put certain questions to him, saying "you said this, you said that". The witness replied as he wanted. You have a right to re-examine, and I see that there are no other questions in that connection. Very well. Let me recapitulate. The statement will be admitted into evidence, it is the only exhibit that will be admitted into evidence. In that case, we can continue. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have one more area of enquiry and that is a videotape which I would like to play. It is quite short. There are three segments, and I have asked that the three segments be played sequentially with a pause in between each of the three. Captain Ellis, with respect to the first segment, I would ask that if during the playing of the first segment, if you are able to identify a location, a Warrior, an UN vehicle or if you recognise a particular scene, a place, that you tell us and that after this segment is played, I will also have some additional questions of you. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So I ask that the first segment of the tape be played. (Videotape played) (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is the end of the first segment. If it could be held on the screen, if possible. While that is coming back, I would like to ask you, Captain Ellis, first did you recognise any of the places or vehicles depicted in this segment of videotape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Shall we play it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us run it back and if we could play it again and you could watch, and if you see any places, events, persons that you recognise, try to make a mental note of it and you can tell us when the segment is concluded or, if you wish, you can tell us as you see it. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the Ahmici mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a Warrior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a Scimitar, that is a Lancer call sign. I believe this to be in the Santici Ahmici area. I think that could be the road around Vitez. I certainly do not recognise him. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we can hold this shot, do you recognise the vehicle depicted partially in this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a Scimitar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who is at the top of a Scimitar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the garb as being UN garb? Blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see that he is actually wearing a blue helmet on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If it is a blue helmet, is that UN garb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What kind of weapon is being handed out of the Scimitar, can you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a shotgun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is that a standard UN-issue firearm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the hooded or turbaned individual to whom the shotgun is being handed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you shed any additional light on this image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from the fact it could be anywhere and anywhen, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the clips on this tape? That is, have you seen them before, have you seen them showed or played before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen -- certainly not this. I believe that the first image of a Scimitar driving past the ruined mosque of Ahmici, I think I might have seen that before. The others I do not believe that I have seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The one that you believe you have seen before, was that shown within the BritBat base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was it shown, what, as a video?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it shown to the forces or was it shown privately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there a viewing of that material or did you see it some other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly was not a cinema viewing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Viewing as within the UNPROFOR forces, or was it a private viewing, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was part of a tape that our battalion made. I cannot say exactly where I saw it, but I probably watched it privately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: A tape that was made with different clips of footage to in some ways remember the service in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to highlight the tape I am talking about, my platoon sergeant helped rescue a load of ITV British television archive from a building and as a favour they cut together some clips as a memory of our tour. I believe that the clip of that Scimitar, which is the same sort of vehicle as the machine here, driving past the broken part of the Ahmici mosque was part of that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you do not recognise this image of an UN soldier handing a shotgun to a hooded or turbaned combatant, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: As we play the next segment, if you could tell us if you recognise any of the persons depicted, where the segment was taken and when, if you would roll the second segment, please, which is very short, perhaps five seconds. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Martyn Thomas, that is Monty Wooley. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the earlier scene of a structure in this segment? Would you like to see it again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why do we not run it back, with the court's permission, it is very short. Play it once more. You will notice the date in the lower right-hand corner, April 16th 1993. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that is Martyn Thomas to the left in the blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Wooley to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he also in your UNPROFOR force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was part of the 9th/12th Lancer squadron attached to 1 Cheshire. He was a troop commander with the squadron, he is a cavalry officer. I do not recognise exactly where that might be. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. The third segment; again, if you could watch and tell us if you recognise any person, any place or the vehicles depicted in this third segment. You can play the third segment, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Jelinak, that is Colonel Stewart's vehicle. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let us play that again perhaps the technical staff could freeze on -- if we could go back there, approximately three scenes, and if we could go back to the first one, yes, and freeze there on the man. Do you recognise this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as an individual, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is he dressed in a typical way a BiH soldier might be dressed, with uniform pants but otherwise civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But you do not know where or when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it runs on to that next scene, if it is not a cut and edited part, it would be in Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It may be cut between them. Let us progress to the second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Jelinak, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To the third depiction, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vehicle you can see in the bottom left would probably be, although I do not know, it is the vehicle that was seen in the frame before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about the vehicle to the right in the middle right of this screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, on the right-hand side. Do you know what kind of vehicle that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a Warrior fighting vehicle and it is a command vehicle and I believe it to be Colonel Stewart's vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Is it firing in this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart's vehicle, did it fire at some point in time that you recognise as being this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, I believe it to be Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the circumstances of that engagement were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that they were being engaged by sniper fire and they identified the sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And fire was returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Colonel Stewart present at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen any of the segments -- excuse me. Have you seen any of the clips from the second and third segments that you have seen before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen the second segment, I have not seen that before. I have not seen a picture of that soldier running -- I have not actually seen this particular view of this clip, although I have seen something that represents the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know, was there a larger body of tape that your UNPROFOR group took, to create, if you will, a video containing certain portions to memorialise, if you will, your tour in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a video produced, as I say, by my platoon sergeant with the help of the ITV camera people. Where that footage is -- it was cut and pasted to create, as you say, a memorial-type video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you say your platoon sergeant, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Sergeant Kujivinsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who has that tape now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a copy of it myself. I do not know who has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it copied and copies made available to persons that wanted it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really, because my platoon sergeant made it solely for A company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Within A company, was it distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not distributed. I know some people did have copies of it. I do not know who has copies of it now, though. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, your microphone, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think portions of the tape were identified by the witness, portions were not. We would need to sort through that. Why do we not look at the record and then we can offer the segments -- we will offer the segments that he identified and we can do that at a later point in time, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That is in accord with the position taken by the Trial Chamber regarding your request of 30th July. In this case the witness has identified some parts of the video, and not identified others. For the present, we will not admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That concludes my examination. Thank you. Thank you, Captain Ellis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. The judges now have a certain number of questions -- no, I am sorry. You see, I am in a hurry to proceed, so it is a fault on the part of the President. I apologise, Mr. Cayley. You already said that you would use your right to re-examine, so Captain, I wanted to release you too quickly, but first the Prosecutor has the right to re-examine after the cross-examination and after that, the judges will have some questions for you. Mr. Cayley, of course, within the scope of the cross-examination only. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Captain Ellis, in your cross-examination you referred to a kidnapping of certain HVO staff officers that occurred in, I think, approximately mid April. At the time, what was your opinion as to why that kidnapping of those HVO staff officers had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was at the time a lot of tension in the area and speaking to other officers within the battalion, and I do not know this first hand, there was a lot of tension in Turbe and Travnik where the Muslim soldiers were having difficulty doing their normal change around on the front-line. They used to orchestrate a changeover of troops, and the general feeling was that they were being prevented to do so by the HVO, and I believe at the time it was generally felt that the reason these kidnappings took place was as a direct result of that anger that they felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So these were Bosnian soldiers on the front-line with the Bosnian Serbs in Turbe, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, that was where they were not being able to effect their changeovers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The HVO were preventing these soldiers coming back from the front-lines and changing over with other soldiers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether that is fact or not. That was the general impression held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Amongst the officers of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated also in your cross-examination, you were trying as best you could to describe the number of houses that you saw on fire in Vitez, and I accept that your memory is now some nearly five years old, but can you make it precise for the court and explain whether or not every house that you saw that morning was on fire, or whether some were on fire, and in fact the state of those houses; if there were houses that were not on fire, what state those houses were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, and I refer now to the whole of the Vitez area, as an overall impression, there were houses on fire. I cannot say exactly which ones were. However, there were also houses that were not on fire. Some of those houses were not touched in any way by bullet pock marks or shrapnel scars, whereas some of the houses on fire were. The impression at the time was that these houses had not been touched at all. They had been touched -- they had not been touched purely because they deliberately did not want to be touched.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that there was a selection process actually taking place at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say that there was a selection, but it did seem strange that some houses were on fire, other houses were riddled with bullets and yet some houses remained untouched.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is it not true that in the course of a battle between two forces engaged with each other, you would expect to see all of the housing damaged by crossfire, by bullet marks; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it was almost a certainty that if rounds were fired, mortar rounds were exploding and there were objectives to be achieved, yes, the majority of buildings in an area would be affected in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, we will move on. A lot of discussion in your cross-examination centred around this phrase that you used of "fighting between the Muslims and the HVO". Did you at any time, in any of these places that you visited on 16th April, see any form of credible defence against the attack that you saw taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In your entire time of service in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you see any dead soldiers at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my memory, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you see any dead civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do not place a number on it, if you cannot. A large number, a small number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In proportion, yes, I definitely saw the results of dead civilians, 20 maybe 30 personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You also mentioned during your cross-examination that you identified the Dubravica school as being the location of the anti-tank recoilless gun that engaged you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think you subsequently visited that school, did you not, with Colonel Stewart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Why did you visit the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there to provide protection. Colonel Stewart was visiting with Claire Pobliovski, who is a RC representative, and their intent was to negotiate a prisoner release. It was my understanding that prisoners were being held by Croat forces and I was purely there to provide protection for that move.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: These prisoners were being held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The feeling was that the Croat forces as a whole were there, although my understanding of it was there were HOS there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony that you encountered a Bosnian tank brigade on the Vitez Zenica road; what was the function of that brigade on that road, did the Bosnian soldiers tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me their task was to keep that road open.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You referred also in your testimony to the fact, both in your examination-in-chief and your cross-examination, that you took General Blaskic to a number of locations in and around Central Bosnia. Were you ever instructed at the time by the battalion why you were taking him to a particular place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The usual outline task was to pick him up. The belief was that he was attending conferences with or hosted by the British battalion, and that was the general reason that we thought behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had seen a large number of troops in Novi Travnik on 15th April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: To which military faction did those troops belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like in Novi Travnik at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of very high tension. There was a very different atmosphere in the air to the remainder of the surrounding area. There was one of tension, it was very atmospheric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There was an atmosphere of expectation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not quite put your finger on it, but something was --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Something was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly so. There was definitely a heightened atmosphere of tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How many troops were there in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say how many troops there were. It was night-time. I saw 10, maybe 15 troops on the road sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of these troops subsequently went to the area of Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You referred, both in your cross-examination and your examination-in-chief, to the garage on the bypass that goes around Vitez. Is there anything particularly significant about that garage? Is there anything that you recall in your memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only reason, apart from its location, was that there was a place next to it, a sort of large building and by it there was a bear in a cage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: When you were in Bosnia, during your service in that area, do you consider the HVO and the HOS to be part of the Bosnian Croat forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were definitely part of the Bosnian Croat forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: One last point, Captain Ellis. I know you are a man of great modesty, but on your left chest there is a small oak leaf, is there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand that, certainly from my own knowledge, that is an official -- an indication of official mention in despatches, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think that is in fact an operational gallantry award that you wear on your chest, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court how you were mentioned in despatches, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I led my platoon across a minefield under shellfire and sustained machine gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Captain Ellis. I would like to ask you some global questions, perhaps to help in my summing-up your extensive, may I say, eyewitness which you spent the last hours telling us. The first thing which I gathered clearly was that all the victims you came across, you saw in burnt houses, whether they were women, children or men, were civilians, am I right in this deduction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, although I could not ascertain whether the people in that burning house were civilians or not because they were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: By the way, in one of the burning houses you said you saw two people sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Were the houses burnt with people inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The inhabitants of these houses were supposed to be military people or just normal citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presumed that they were normal citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But the others you saw, you came across, you mentioned women, children and so on, they were apparently civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Civilians. You mentioned that HVO moved in Jelinak and you even used the words "butchered and tortured people", as well as in Sivrino Selo, also in Ahmici, the mosque was destroyed and in Santici there were damages and in many places there were massive explosions. Were these places or others, were they in any way places of resistance, or was this required by, to say, military necessities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the village areas, Santici, Sivrino Selo, Ahmici were purely civilian villages with no tactical importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So there was no obvious reason for the attacking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I would like also to ask you, the structure -- the nature of the action you mentioned in your eyewitness testimony indicates that the attacks were by disciplined soldiers, or were they by hoodlums and undisciplined groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only real action that I saw being fought was in the town of Vitez and I believe that action was conducted in a disciplined and organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Forgive me if I ask you to talk a little louder, because I am not having my earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only real troop movement and offensive action I saw being fought was in Vitez. I believe that the nature of the operation they were conducting required command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Also the nature of the weapons, apparently some of them were highly sophisticated. I am not a military man, I could not understand what you explained, but they were apparently highly sophisticated. Would that be in the hands of normal people, or of disciplined military troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that that one weapon that I saw, the anti-tank rocket, was so out of place in the normal environs of Vitez that yes, there were more sophisticated weaponry than you would expect to see in normal militia and local-type troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you notice any, what can I say, parallelism in the attacks which indicate that there was a planning and an organisation of the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was an organised operation for a number of reasons, the first of which I believe to be the seizure of key points. The key points in this instance were the garage and the blocking off of the Vitez road, for whatever reason. Secondly, the fact that bodies of troops were walking down the road to Vitez indicates that there was a grouping system, and secondly, orchestrated fighting, as I have already described, within the town of Vitez. Lastly, the fact that the actual re-supply of ammunition to the area would have had to have required a logistic chain that would have had to have been planned beforehand and therefore, yes, I believe it was a pre-planned and commanded operation throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You say "commanded". Have you an idea in whose hand was the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who actually commanded that operation, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the general commander of the area in which all these eyewitness testimony relates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding is that Blaskic was the regional commander of the area, the area basically being that which runs from Vitez through to Busovaca and down to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain Ellis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Captain, I shall not keep you very long. My first question is tacked on to Judge Riad's first question. That is, you saw various places under attack on 16th April; in these various places, did you see any defensive arrangements, I imagine such as barbed wire or sand-bagging, or manholes or ditches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That would apply also to Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any purpose-built defences, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You transported General Blaskic, I think, on 15 or 16 occasions, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be an approximate figure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your impression was that on each occasion he went to attend conferences with the British battalion, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and it was either a pick-up to take him to or a drop-off to take him from those particular meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Would it also be your impression that the purpose of those discussions was to arrange in some manner or the other to diffuse tension in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I believe the sole purpose of those meetings was to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now then, did you ever transport anyone from HOS to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Within your knowledge, did any other transporting agency that you know of also transport any HOS people to those conferences with the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I am aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The British battalion tended to liaise with General Blaskic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case. It would have to be clarified by a senior officer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Was he the senior officer on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my understanding, yes. The Croatian forces in the area were as a whole commanded by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am a little interested in the relations between HOS and the HVO, so can you tell me, you said you saw General Blaskic in black. Did HOS also use black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You spent some time on the ground in the Vitez area, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 16th in my vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: What about other times during your stay in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to go into Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did HOS in any way co-operate with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see the HOS in Vitez; however, I did see the HOS mixing quite freely with HVO troops in the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which was the larger body of men, the HOS or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You said you saw three houses burning in the vicinity of the catholic church, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to how those houses might have been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not in possession of any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: HOS had its headquarters where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the HOS headquarters -- in fact, I do not know where the HOS headquarters was. I know their main rest area, or the main area where they used to be, was an area past Ahmici on the left-hand side of the road in an old cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How far is that from the Hotel Vitez in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four, possibly five, six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are a military man, and you have had experience in planning, I think you said, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Within your knowledge, was it within the capacity of HOS to stage an operation on its own which resulted in the kind of damage which you saw on 16th and 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on its own, no. They could have taken one objective out of the many that we saw, but not on its own as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Captain, the Trial Chamber wishes to thank you for the totality of your testimony to the Prosecutor and the Defence and also in answering the questions of my colleagues. Your appearance before this Tribunal is ended and the Tribunal wishes to thank you for your contribution. Mr. Registrar, will you please have the witness accompanied out and after that, it will be almost 5.30, so I think the Prosecutor can tell us what we are going to do tomorrow. Please accompany the witness, Mr. Usher. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On a housekeeping note, if I could formally apply for admission of five exhibits which I have not formally applied for. They are exhibits 105, 106 and 107, and exhibits 50D and 56D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could counsel just describe those for me, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is the photograph of the artillery piece next to the church and the two buildings in Sivrino Selo. We can identify where they come from, if the Registrar requires the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection as to the three photos. And the other two, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The other two are the aerial photographs that we looked at after lunch with the markings on where you were content --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of tomorrow's proceedings, Mr. President, yes, we do have another witness with which we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will there be any protective measures for that witness so we do not waste any time tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there will be no protective measures required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. (Pause). Very well. You know that there was a plenary meeting of judges that was to be held on Friday, it has been adjourned and therefore the Trial Chamber can sit on Thursday and Friday under normal conditions. The session is adjourned, we will meet tomorrow at 10.00. (5.30 pm) (Court adjourned until 10.00 am the following day) 21 22 23 24 25
